name: The Queers
label: Lookout!
lede: Joe King kept rewriting the Ramones' songbook for forty years, and a drunken 24-hour session in Indiana gave pop-punk its best-selling Lookout! record.

eras.title: A basement in Portsmouth
eras.text: Joe King, Scott Gildersleeve and Jack Hayes start a Ramones-worshipping band in New Hampshire. It lasts about six shows, but the name and the songs stick.

years.h: Three friends and a basement in Portsmouth, New Hampshire
years.p: Joe King (Joe Queer), Scott Gildersleeve (Tulu) and Jack Hayes (Wimpy Rutherford) form The Queers, rehearsing in Tulu's basement and covering The Dave Clark Five, The Monkees and the [[Ramones|d6ed7887-a401-47a8-893c-34b967444d26]].
years.xp: Wikipedia's account has Tulu introducing the others to the Ramones in 1976. King had also spent time in Manhattan Beach, California, seeing LA punk bands including [[Black Flag|9941a936-196a-4a62-ae53-a69cbc33f20e]] and the Germs, and came home fired up.

years.h: Tulu writes "We'd Have a Riot Doing Heroin" in about two minutes
years.p: After hearing Black Flag's TV Party and Angry Samoans' The Queer Pills, the band starts writing originals. Wikipedia describes Tulu's heroin-titled song as their first signature tune.

years.h: Bassist Keith Hages joins; six shows follow
years.p: The lineup plays roughly six gigs in Portsmouth and Portland, Maine, before breaking up in late 1984. The Love Me and Kicked Out of the Webelos EPs come from this stretch.

eras.title: Joe tries again
eras.text: King rebuilds the band with new players. A four-year run ends when he buys a restaurant instead of making a record.

years.h: Joe King re-forms The Queers with Hugh O'Neill on drums
years.p: J.J. Rassler joins on guitar and Kevin Kecy on bass. O'Neill will be the band's drummer for most of the next decade.

years.h: Joe King buys a restaurant and the band stops
years.p: The 1985 lineup ends when King takes on the restaurant, per Wikipedia. It is a very short retirement.

eras.title: Lookout! and the Ramones-core blueprint
eras.text: With O'Neill and new bassist B-Face, King makes Grow Up, wins over Ben Weasel, and lands on Larry Livermore's Lookout! label, where the band makes its best-known records.

years.h: Back with Hugh O'Neill and B-Face
years.p: King rebuilds again with O'Neill, bassist B-Face and rhythm guitarist Sean Rowley, who leaves for art school the same year.

years.h: Grow Up on Shakin' Street Records
years.p: The debut album gets the band noticed around New England and, eventually, by [[Screeching Weasel|e4a135d0-1948-4620-bc07-b0217d09ccc1]]'s [[Ben Weasel|bdce6736-8bc6-4818-8fd7-781822b674a9]].

years.h: Ben Weasel becomes an early champion
years.p: Wikipedia says Weasel befriended King around 1991, and King sent a demo to Lookout! head [[Larry Livermore|427f8569-3791-4887-976c-242bb49a573f]], who heard doo-wop and Beach Boys melodies in it.

years.cap: The Queers around Love Songs for the Retarded
years.src: Wikipedia: Love Songs for the Retarded
years.h: Twenty-four hours in Lafayette, Indiana
years.p: [[Mass Giorgini|abcbcb2a-f783-4300-ba85-3cb1a32c6b2b]] engineers the band at Sonic Iguana Studio and Ben Weasel produces. Most songs for Love Songs for the Retarded are done in one or two takes.
years.xp: Livermore later wrote that the album cover, a bleary-eyed band surrounded by bottles, showed what the session looked like. The band arrived drunk but rehearsed.

years.h: Love Songs for the Retarded, their Lookout! debut
years.p: The band's best-selling album, past 100,000 copies according to Wikipedia. A 2007 Asian Man reissue is remixed and remastered.

years.h: Shout at the Queers live album
years.p: Jay Adelberg fills in on drums for the live record, while Hugh O'Neill and King struggle with heroin. The band stages an intervention for O'Neill and pauses playing.

years.h: Touring with Screeching Weasel and Rancid
years.p: The band hits the road behind Love Songs with two of the biggest bands on the Lookout! and Epitaph circuit.

years.h: Beat Off, recorded in a week in Chicago
years.p: Ben Weasel produces at Flat Iron Studios, April 1-7. Screeching Weasel's Dan Panic plays drums while O'Neill is out with addiction.
years.xp: Wikipedia reports that Dan Vapid's guitar and backing vocals were removed from the final mix by Weasel. Vapid says he only learned this when royalties never came. Weasel wanted a no-frills sound, while King and Livermore wanted fuller arrangements, which led to the Surf Goddess EP later that summer.

years.h: They re-record the Ramones' Rocket to Russia in full
years.p: Jay Adelberg drums on the note-for-note tribute to the band's biggest influence.

years.h: Move Back Home with Hugh O'Neill back
years.p: O'Neill recovers and returns for the album.

years.h: Surf Goddess EP, with richer arrangements
years.p: King and Livermore get the fuller sound they wanted after Beat Off. Dan Vapid returns on guitar.

years.h: Don't Back Down reunites King, B-Face and O'Neill
years.p: J.J. Rassler comes back on guitar. It is the band's last Lookout! record of the decade.

years.h: An Epitaph offer splits the trio
years.p: King wants to take Epitaph's three-album offer. B-Face and Hugh O'Neill oppose it, and King replaces them with Dave Swain and Chris Fields.
years.xp: Per Wikipedia, King favored the deal while his bandmates did not. Swain, from Jon Cougar Concentration Camp, takes bass and Chris Fields of The Dwarves takes drums. B-Face goes on to Chixdiggit!, the Mopes and The Groovie Ghoulies.

eras.title: Joe and whoever's in the van
eras.text: King is the only fixed point as bassists and drummers rotate. The band moves among labels, loses O'Neill, and finally fights Lookout! over royalties.

years.h: Punk Rock Confidential
years.p: The band makes its first album after the Lookout! run, with Dave Swain on bass (1998-2002).

years.h: Hugh O'Neill dies of brain cancer
years.p: The drummer on the band's Lookout! classics dies January 20 at age 41, according to Wikipedia. King later said O'Neill was dying while Larry Livermore was selling the label.

years.h: Beyond the Valley...
years.p: A record made while the lineup keeps shifting.

years.h: Pleasant Screams
years.p: King tells Razorcake that the band left Lookout! for Hopeless and later came back, saying "friends have fights."
years.xp: In a 2002 Razorcake interview King said the band sold more records at Hopeless but did not make as much money. He was also planning an autobiography, tentatively titled Get Out of the Van.

years.h: The Queers take their masters back from Lookout!
years.p: After six albums on Lookout!, the band reclaims its master recordings, alleging breach of contract over unpaid royalties.
years.xp: The reclaimed masters allow remixed reissues of records like Love Songs for the Retarded and Beat Off on Asian Man Records in 2007.

eras.title: Still Joe Queer
eras.text: Under Asian Man Records the band keeps recording and touring, with a rotating cast and Joe King the only constant.

years.h: Munki Brain for Asian Man Records
years.p: The first new album after the masters fight. Their "Wipe Out" cover also appears in the film Surf's Up.

years.h: Dave Swain rejoins on bass
years.p: He stays until 2015.

years.h: God Save the Queers tribute album
years.p: Dwarves, Screeching Weasel, Teengenerate and New Bomb Turks are among the bands covering them.

years.h: Back to the Basement
years.p: A steadier lineup for the band.

years.h: Joe Queer's Ferguson posts draw fire
years.p: Wikipedia reports King posted support for a police officer after Michael Brown's death. Don Giovanni's Joe Steinhardt asked labels to drop the band, and King challenged him to a filmed debate.

years.h: Save the World
years.p: A late-career record from the New Hampshire trio.

years.h: Reverberation
years.p: The band's latest album on the Wikipedia discography.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Love Songs for the Retarded
